description.narrative: Gini index measures the extent to which the distribution of income (or, in some cases, consumption expenditure) among individuals or households within an economy deviates from a perfectly equal distribution. A Lorenz curve plots the cumulative percentages of total income received against the cumulative number of recipients, starting with the poorest individual or household. The Gini index measures the area between the Lorenz curve and a hypothetical line of absolute equality, expressed as a percentage of the maximum area under the line. Thus a Gini index of 0 represents perfect equality, while an index of 100 implies perfect inequality.

description.narrative: I1.3 Corruption Perceptions Index

comment.narrative: Regarding the Indicator 1.3 we remember that the Corruption Perception Index registers the perception among Albania based on how corrupt their public sector is perceived to be on a scale of 0100 where 0 means highly corrupt and 100 means very clean. In 2023 we registered a slight improvement of this indicator 36 to 37. This value allows us to develop a twofold reflection. On the one hand we can assume a more trustful perception related to transparency in Albania in the public sector.On the other hand we can affirm a greater awareness on the part of the interviewees with respect to being able to identify and recognise corrupt phenomena. This element represents the first key factor in the fight against corruption. However the data still suggest the need for a continuous and careful monitoring of decisionmaking and public processes in Albania. In this regard we believe that the experiences of SEs that we are supporting with TWIST both in confiscated assets from organised crime and in response to the needs of the territory can be concrete examples of transparency rights and a clean economy.This ethical model to be inspired by as opposed to the corrupt model was also widely understood during the study visit to Italy. On this occasion the representative of the SEs had the opportunity to see the great impact of the social reuse of confiscated assets from mafias and organised crime as generative tools to build an inclusive society and a clean economy. Telling positive experiences of this kind we believe can incentivize the trust in the construction of a fairer and more transparent society.

title.narrative: Number of individuals from key national and local authorities and Civil Society Organizations (CSOs) trained by the EUfunded intervention who increased their knowledge and/or skills for preventing and countering corruption, or organised crime, or violent extremism or environmental crime

description.narrative: For purposes of this indicator, a CSO is understood as a nongovernmental, notforprofit entity. It should ideally have a compatible legal personality (i.e. registered as such). However, the EU considers civil society organisations to embrace a wide range of actors with multiple roles and mandates which includes all nonState, notforprofit, independent and nonviolent structures, through which people organise to pursue shared objectives and ideals, whether political, cultural, religious, environmental, social or economic or related to health. They include, but are not limited to: Nongovernmental organisations, organisations representing indigenous peoples, womens and youth organisations, diaspora organisations, migrants organisations, local traders associations and citizens groups, cooperatives, employers associations and trade unions (social partners), organisations representing economic and social interests, organisations fighting corruption and fraud and promoting good governance, civil rights organisations and organisations combating discrimination, local organisations (including networks) involved in decentralised regional cooperation and integration, consumer organisations, environmental, teaching, cultural, research and scientific organisations, universities, churches and religious associations and communities, philosophical and nonconfessional organisations, the notforprofit media and any nongovernmental associations and independent foundations, including independent political foundations.The individual should be a recognised member of a national / local authority or CSO, and have been the beneficiary of training delivered by an intervention that has been financed fully or partly by IPA.The individuals should demonstrate an increased level of knowledge or skills in the areas in which they have been trained. Failure to demonstrate this means they should not be counted for purposes of this indicator. Therefore, relevant interventions must foresee an internal learning evaluation system that foresees the possibility to demonstrate knowledge or skills acquired.Training can take any form or combination of competence based transfer of knowledge and skill (theoretical, practical; teaching, coaching, mentoring, peer learning, etc), as long as it is focused on ensuring that a set of competencies (alternative term for attitude, knowledge and skill) is imparted and integrated.The areas of training are directly dealing with preventing and countering the following: Corruption, Organised crime, Violent extremism, Environmental crimeLocal authorities means municipal (or higher regional/provincial) public authorities or their agencies. National authorities means any national level public authorities or their agencies.

comment.narrative: At least 80 of targetgroup state to understand the relevance and assignation mechanism of confiscated assets for social purposes.

Thanks to the questionnaires filled in the framework of the Study Visit in Italy A.1.2.3 by the representative of the 10 SEs and by Tirana Municipality representative we registered a positive improvement related to the comprehension of the relevance and assignation mechanism of confiscated assets for social purposes I.2.2. Indeed during the study visit in Italy the Albanian SEs delegation had the opportunity to get to know about 8 experiences of social entrepreneurship established in confiscated property in Italy and to confront themselves with these experiences. As detailed in the dedicated paragraf particular attention was paid to the selection of Italian social enterprise experiences to be met. The selection was made on the basis of common activities and objectives with the social enterprises supported by Twist. This element was strongly pursued in order to facilitate the interaction and comparison between the two different experiences and to strengthen the common elements. Indeed starting from the Italian experience on the promotion of social reuse of confiscated assets one of the most important factors to enhance this good practice is to create collaborative networks among the SEs. This particular element has been enhanced even from the participation of the Argentine Delegation of Bien Restituido project another EuropeAid project on the promotion of social reuse of confiscated assets in Argentina carried out by Libera.On the basis of these elements it can be assumed that the study visit to Italy raised awareness among CSOs and the Tirana Municipality of the role of social enterprises both as a model within confiscated assets and as a civic tool in the fight against organised crime not only at local and national level but also at international level.
